256	Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.
257	
258	**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
259	  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
260	  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
261	  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
262	  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
263	  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
264	  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".
265	
266	New read models, added to the wire crate:
267	
268	- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
269	- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
270	- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
271	- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
272	  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
273	  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
274	  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
275	  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
276	  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
277	  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
278	  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
279	- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.
280	
281	Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.
282	
283	### 4.4 WebSocket events
284	
285	Envelope:
286	
287	```json
288	{
289	  "server_id": "uuid",
290	  "epoch": "uuid",
291	  "revision": 1042,
292	  "type": "changed",
293	  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
294	  "at_ms": 1760220000000
295	}
296	```
297	
298	Event types:
299	
300	- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
301	- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
302	- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
303	- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
304	- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
305	- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.
306	
307	**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:
308	
309	1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
310	2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
311	   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
312	   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
313	   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
314	   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
315	   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
316	3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
317	
318	**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.
319	
320	**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
321	
322	**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:
323	
324	1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
325	2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
326	3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
327	4. enables commands.
328	
329	Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.
330	
331	### 4.5 Commands
332	
333	- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
334	- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
335	- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.
336	- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
337	  - `done`: use the reply;
338	  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
339	  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.
340	  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.
341	- `send` puts keys into the pane, as the app's own message box does. "Accepted" means the keys were sent. Progress is the record's state: `PromptSubmitted`, then working, then `Stop` with the new last response. A send to a pane sitting at Claude Code's folder trust question is accepted but goes nowhere until `trust` answers it; the session view carries `trust_question`, and the client shows the same "Trust this folder" button the app shows.
342	- `resume` on a not-running agent is user-initiated, so allowed, but the client confirms it ("Resume spends a turn") before sending; the host never resumes on its own.
343	- Failures name the reason: not running, not resumable, unknown record, scope missing, pairing revoked, log unavailable.
344	- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. The reply is the command body with `made: [{kind: "session", id}]`; `/ops/{op}` carries `made` too, so a creation whose reply was lost still names its record. `info` lists `create`. The client offers it on a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves `create`: a plus button on the Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session, opening a sheet with the host, the project by workspace, the kind, a name (the kind's word and a count when none is typed), a directory and the first message; Start posts it, reads the project's sessions again and opens the new session's window.
345	
346	**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.
347	
348	- `GET sessions/{id}/draft` (any paired device) answers `{draft: {text, live, status, status_text, can_undo, can_redo, ai, busy}}`: the rendered text, the byte range of the utterance still being recognized or null, the editor's status (`idle`, `listening`, `finishing`, `degraded`, `error`) with its reason, whether undo and redo apply, whether the host has an `OpenAI` key for the AI pass, and whether a pass is running. Only an agent session has a draft (`no_draft` otherwise). The host emits `changed {draft, id}` for an editor whose draft moved, fingerprinted a few times a second while a subscriber is connected, and a device holding the draft re-reads it; no watch is needed, since the editor is the host's own state rather than a source the worker polls.
349	- `POST sessions/{id}/draft` (control) applies one of the editor's tools and answers with the draft as it stands: `{action: "replace", text}` sets the text whole (what the device typed; last writer wins, one person), `undo`, `redo`, `clear`, `clean_up` (the AI pass, refused `failed` when the host has no key), `delete_sentence`, `delete_paragraph`, and `{action: "send", op}`, which takes the draft's text to the pane exactly as `session.send` does, under the device's op as the key, and clears the editor when it went; a repeat of a send that went is answered from the log. A send of an empty draft is refused.
350	- `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` (control) carries `{session, events}`: the device's recognizer session, a number the device picks apart from the host's own, and its speech events in order, each `{sequence, kind, utterance, revision, text}` with `kind` one of `started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`, `voice_ended`, `stopped`. The host feeds them to the editor as its own recognizer's events: `started` puts the editor's status at listening, a partial is the provisional span revised in place, a final commits the utterance at its anchor, `stopped` returns the status to idle. At most 256 events of 16 KiB each per request. The reply is the draft as it stands, so the device sees its words land without waiting for the event. The device segments speech into utterances itself (the Apple recognizer starts over after a pause and closes an utterance by re-sending its words later); the editor keeps the document. Two recognizers into one editor (the desk's and the headset's) are kept apart by their session numbers.
351	
352	### 4.6 Dispatch and waiting
353	
354	"Waiting on you" on a card includes reasons set from outside: Dispatch marks a session through `session.waiting` when one of its tickets needs a decision. `SessionView.waiting_reason` is already on the wire; the client shows it. The `Dispatch · <project>` working sets are ordinary sets to the client.
355	
356	#### 4.7 Tickets
357	
358	The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.
359	
360	Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.
361	
362	The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.
363	
364	## 5. Security and pairing
365	
366	A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
367	
368	- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
369	- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
370	- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
371	- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
372	- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
373	- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
374	- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
375	- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
376	- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
377	- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
378	- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
379	- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
380	- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
381	- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.
382	
383	## 6. Discovery and connection lifecycle
384	
385	### 6.1 Discovery
386	
387	- The host advertises `_switchboard._tcp` while listening on a LAN interface.
388	- The Apple client browses with `Network.framework`.
389	- `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` and `NSBonjourServices` (`_switchboard._tcp`) in the Apple app manifests.
390	- Manual host and port entry for networks where mDNS is blocked.
391	- Known servers and pinned identities are persisted separately from transient discovery results.
392	- A changed IP address is not a new server.

# Lessons from Prompt Box

Prompt Box was the first app built from the original scaffold: a voice
dictation tool on top of whisper.cpp, egui, and OpenAI, built over two days
with an AI coding agent. These are the things that made it go well, in the
order they mattered. The template bakes in the ones that can be baked in.

## Architecture

**Put a deterministic core behind an action/effect boundary from day one.**
The scaffold started with logic as plain methods on the app struct. The
first real feature (streaming speech with provisional text) made it clear
that a state machine with explicit inputs (`AppAction`), explicit outputs
(`Effect`), and an injected `Clock` was the only way to test timing
behavior without sleeping. Every later feature slotted into that shape:
voice commands, AI rewrites on worker threads, tool plugins, toasts. Around
ninety core tests ran in well under a second. The template ships this
shape with one trivial feature in it so the pattern is there to copy.

**Ports and adapters earn their keep on the second adapter.** Clipboard,
file store, speech engine, typist, rewriter: each got a trait, a real
implementation, and a fake. The fakes made headless UI tests possible on
CI and let the whole app run in a "Debug" mode with scripted dictation and
no model. Write the fake at the same time as the real adapter, in the same
file.

**Keep `ui.rs` dumb.** Edit diffing and keyboard shortcuts were the only
logic that had to live near egui, and even those produce actions. When a
bug showed up, it was almost always reproducible as a core test.

## Process

**Spike risky technology in a throwaway crate first.** Before Milestone 1,
a standalone `spikes/voice-spike` crate answered whether whisper.cpp could
stream on this machine, what the real API looked like, and how long the
first Metal shader compile takes. Its README recorded the findings. The
spike's fixtures were reused as test inputs later.

**Milestones, each a working app.** Shell, then microphone, then editing
operations, then voice commands, then AI, then projects. Each milestone was
one commit with the README updated. Scope stayed honest because the app
had to run at every step.

**Write the design doc, then stop consulting it.** A product design doc
set priorities ("never silently lose speech" first). It was useful for
ordering milestones and for the layering diagram in `lib.rs`. Beyond that
the code and README became the source of truth, and the doc was left as
history.

**Pre-commit hook plus CI, both running the same three commands.** Nothing
formatted wrong, lint-dirty, or failing ever landed. The hook never modifies
files; it just says no. Clippy pedantic caught real mistakes and taught
idioms along the way. The two `allow`s in `Cargo.toml` are the only lints
that were pure noise.

**Audit comments once features settle.** Halfway through, a pass removed
comments that restated the code or narrated which milestone added what.
The rule since: comments say why.

## Tooling facts that cost time

- egui 0.36 renamed the `App` trait method to `ui`, merged panels into one
  `Panel` type, and kittest needs `.focus()` before `type_text`. See
  `CLAUDE.md`. When docs and compiler disagree, read the crate source in
  `~/.cargo/registry`.
- eframe 0.36 runs `App::logic`, not `App::ui`, while the window is
  occluded or minimized; anything that must keep ticking belongs in
  `logic`. The symptom looked like a sleep bug: the control port went
  silent until the window was uncovered.
- The crate forbids `unsafe`, and that survived native AppKit calls
  (Dock badge) because `objc2` exposes safe wrappers for the common
  methods. Put such code in a tiny `cfg`-gated adapter.
- macOS ties the Accessibility grant to the code signature, so an ad-hoc
  signed app loses the grant on every rebuild. A self-signed "Code Signing"
  certificate fixes it. The bundle script and README in Prompt Box have the
  recipe.
- A bundled `.app` starts with `/` as its working directory, so reading a
  `.env` from the current directory silently fails. Read secrets from a
  settings file in the platform data directory instead, with `.env` as a
  dev-only fallback.
- Two monitors: `screencapture -x a.png b.png` captures both; one path
  only gives the primary display.
- Linux CI for eframe needs `libxkbcommon-dev libgtk-3-dev libssl-dev`;
  audio adds `libasound2-dev`, whisper adds `cmake`.
# Switchboard Remote Client Architecture — v1

**Status:** Proposed implementation specification, revised against the repository
**Targets:** Switchboard Rust host; native visionOS client; reusable iPadOS client core
**Primary objective:** Browse and interact with the sessions and working sets of multiple independently running Switchboard instances, with native spatial windows on visionOS.

## 0. Revision notes

The first draft was written without the codebase. This revision merges its
concepts with what exists:

- "Cards" are not a resource. A working-set item is a `PinTarget` (a session
  record id, or a project id and a path relative to the project root) with a
  grid rectangle; the target is the item's identity. The API speaks
  **sessions, projects, working sets with pins, and files reachable only
  through a pin**. There is no `card_id`.
- The control port (`control/`, `switchboard-control`) already carries most of
  this API: `SessionView`, `SetView` with `Pin`s, `ProjectView`, `waiting`,
  `session.screen`, `session.send`, `session.resume`, `session.trust`, and
  `find` / `op.status`. The remote port is a transport over that contract,
  not a second one.
- The control port's operation id and `operations.log` are the idempotency
  mechanism, extended so that a non-replayable command is logged **before**
  it runs (today only creations are logged, and only after).
- The host has no Tokio and no HTTP stack. The core is single-threaded and
  every request is answered on the frame thread; the remote port keeps that
  shape, with bounded queues.
- The host has no event bus, and its transcript and screen polling follows
  the local view. The port adds a watch set of its own, app-level content
  caches that version what they read, a per-process revision counter and
  "changed" events with refetch, computed by diffing the exported read
  models after every pass rather than by watching for a save. Clients
  subscribe before they snapshot.
- Security is bound by the repo's existing rules (CLAUDE.md "Hard rules",
  design.md "Trust boundary"): one redaction policy covers every text that
  leaves the port and runs before any cut, host key material lives in the
  Keychain, the certificate
  is verified out of band before pairing, and agents are never resumed
  without a human.
- A spike precedes Milestone A, and no milestone ships a LAN-bound
  unauthenticated port.

The second review round (the outside reviewer's F1–F6, and a trim) changed
this:

- Collections are answered whole with bounded fields; the membership
  snapshot walk is gone. Only the conversation pages.
- The watch set is capped globally with least-recently-read eviction; there
  is no `watch_refused` and no "not live" client state.
- Content work (parsing, file reads, masking, hashing) runs on the
  connection thread, never on the frame; the frame hands out the handle and
  the policy and records the version. The frame does core state only.
- Content versions for files and logs are inode, ctime and size, not mtime
  and length (F2). Pairing codes, tokens, attempt counting and key rotation
  are specified (F3). The client keeps content in memory only (F5). A client
  workspace may span hosts (F6).
- Milestone A is five commits, A0 to A4, with a two-host read-only client at
  A2 (F1).

## 1. Product goals
## 3. Core architecture

```text
Mac A: Switchboard + remote port --\
                                     \       Bonjour + HTTPS/WSS
Mac B: Switchboard + remote port ----> Native Client (visionOS / iPadOS)
                                     /       ConnectionManager
Mac C: Switchboard + remote port --/        UnifiedStore
                                             Window/PresentationStore
```

Each host is authoritative for its own resources. The client aggregates views without copying ownership of sessions. One client maintains **one connection state machine and one WebSocket per connected host**. A host going offline must not block other hosts.

### 3.1 Identity and namespacing

- `server_id`: stable, randomly generated UUID persisted in `<data dir>/identity.json` (its own small file beside `views.json`, so it needs no `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump; written through the store's atomic path). Never derive it from hostname, IP, or Bonjour instance name. A second instance pointed at another `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` therefore has its own.
- `identity.json` also holds the host's **certificate** (DER, base64) and the certificate's creation time. The certificate is public; its private key is in the Keychain (§5). The two are made together, once, on first listen. If the key is missing when the certificate is present (a Keychain reset, an unsigned build), the host makes a fresh pair, logs that it did, and the paired-devices dialog says every pairing is now invalid.
- `server_name`: user-editable display name, kept in `identity.json` beside the id (A1 chose this over a `Settings` field, which would have needed a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and a migrate step for one string). The listen preference (loopback or the local network, and the port) lives there too: the file is the remote port's own, read before the app's records matter.
- Host-side identifiers are the existing ones and are never renamed on the wire: `RecordId` (a session, stable forever), `ProjectId`, `SetId` (a working set, in `views.json`), `SpaceId`. The host id (the tmux session) and the resume handle (the provider's session id) are never exposed as identity; `resume_id` is informational, as on `SessionView`.
- All client-facing references are **qualified**: `(server_id, resource_id)`. A `SessionRef` is `{server_id, record_id}`, a `WorkingSetRef` is `{server_id, set_id}`, a `FileRef` is `{server_id, project_id, path}`.
- A single client may show items from multiple servers in one collection, but every command is routed to the item's owning server.
- `server_id` identifies a logical installation, **not a trusted cryptographic identity**. Trust is the pinned public key established at pairing (§5).

### 3.2 Multi-instance behaviors

- Maintain a list of **known servers** (paired and manually added), independent of currently discovered servers.
- Discovery adds candidates; it does not automatically trust or authorize them.
- Client can connect to all enabled known servers concurrently, reconnecting each independently.
- Default unified view includes items from all connected servers; filter by one or more servers.
- Show a source-machine label on each card, with a clear offline/stale state.
- When a host disconnects, keep its last known items visible as **read-only cached snapshots** with a disconnected indicator. Do not imply that actions succeeded.
- When a host reconnects, reconcile the host's authoritative state before re-enabling commands.
- Preserve the selected server filters and window/item references across client relaunches.
- If two endpoints advertise the same `server_id`, treat them as candidate addresses for one logical server; verify the pinned key before switching endpoints. Do not silently merge untrusted installations.

## 4. Rust host

### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions

- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.
